item.caption:
Tomorrow is Election Day, and I’m not going to pretend this one isn’t personal.

I’m a gay man, a son, a grandchild, and a friend to the women this affects. Amendment 3 isn’t an abstract ballot line to me. It’s people I love.

I put my whole ballot in this carousel, line by line, so nobody has to walk in blind. Swipe through, screenshot the last slide, and bring it with you.

One thing before you go: please do your own research. Read the official ballot language, look up every race, and don’t base your votes only on me. These are just the picks I believe are the most morally, ethically, and politically right. You decide for yourself.

THE OFFICIAL MISSOURI BALLOT LANGUAGE IS LINKED IN MY BIO. PLEASE READ IT, AND THOROUGHLY 

Polls are open 6 a.m. to 7 p.m. Bring a friend. 🏳️‍🌈

#MissouriVotes #VoteNoOn3 #Amendment3 #ElectionDay

author: detricejohnson_realtor

item.authorHandle: detricejohnson_realtor
item.caption:
Madison County, tomorrow is Election Day! 🗳️🇺🇸

Tuesday, November 3, 2026 is the General Election, and Madison County has a full ballot. It’s more than the big races at the top:

✅ U.S. Senate
✅ U.S. House (2nd and 3rd Congressional Districts)
✅ Court of Appeals, Chancery and Circuit Court judges
✅ Madison County Judge, Places 1 and 2
✅ School Board seats

The local races often shape our neighborhoods, schools and courts the most, so look over the whole ballot before you go.

📍 Not sure where you vote? Look up your polling place and see your sample ballot on the Mississippi Secretary of State’s “My Election Day” portal at sos.ms.gov. Ballots differ by precinct, so check yours.

🖊️ When you mark your ballot: Fill in the oval completely with a black or blue pen. Don’t cross out or erase. If you make a mistake, ask for a new ballot.

Whatever your choices, your voice matters in the community we all call home. 🇺🇸

Detrice Johnson, Broker Associate
Keller Williams Realty

☎️ Office: 601-977-9411

item.caption:
This weekend I knocked on doors in Ohio for Sherrod Brown. The people I met — LGBTQ and straight — wanted the same things: affordable lives, good schools, and a fair shot for them and their families.

Tomorrow, that conversation goes to the ballot box across the country:

🗳 Michigan: Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, who ran Detroit’s Ryan White HIV program, is running for Senate with HRC PAC’s endorsement. Nearly 11% of Michigan adults are LGBTQ+.
🗳 Virginia: Voters can remove the same-sex marriage ban from the state constitution. I grew up there, and my family still lives there.🗳 Arizona, Colorado, Missouri, Nebraska and Washington: Ballot measures put kids’ rights up for a public vote. One in Washington would require *all* girls to medically certify their sex to play sports. Rules about who counts reach every kid.
🗳️ From AZ to NY to NH to CA, openly LGBTQ candidates stand poised to make history — and deliver pro-equality majorities.
 
Gay, lesbian, bi, trans: our rights have always been connected — to each other and to our neighbors — and so are our futures.

We live in every zip code and work every job. Please vote tomorrow, and bring someone with you. Visit hrc.org for resources. 

#Vote #ElectionDay #LGBTQ #Equality

author: honesthistory

item.authorHandle: honesthistory
item.caption:
Who doesn't love stickers? ✨ While the exact origin of the I VOTED stickers that pop up throughout the United States on Election Day is unknown, most agree that these stickers became popular in the 1980's. ⁠
⁠
Aside from a brief mention in a 1950 edition of the Miami Herald, the earliest documentation of these stickers came from a 1982 Miami Herald article that mentioned stores providing discounts to shoppers wearing I VOTED stickers. In 1985, the Phoenix Board of Realtors designed and distributed their own polling stickers, also considered one of the earliest designs. In 1987, one of the most well-recognized I VOTED emblems, a white, oval sticker featuring a waving flag and "I Voted" in a serif font, was designed by the president of an election supply company who wanted to remind busy potential voters that Election Day had arrived.⁠
⁠
Before stickers, though, there were ribbons. One earlier piece of US election memorabilia is a ribbon from the 1920 election that read "Under the 19th Amendment I cast my first vote Nov. 2nd, 1920". Just 76 days prior, the 19th Amendment had been ratified, stating that "The rights of citizens of the United States to vote shall not be denied or abridged by the United States or by any State on account of sex."⁠
⁠
Today, I VOTED stickers remain one of the strongest pieces of nonpartisan election memorabilia, worn and posted by voters across the United States every Election Day. Some counties throughout the United States even hold competitions for the design of that year's polling sticker, encouraging excited friends and family of the designer to post their own photos of their loved one's design.⁠
⁠
What would your I VOTED sticker look like? ✨⁠
⁠
#IVoted #Vote #ElectionDay #Stickers

If you want to see change, you've got to be willing to be part of it!

I showed up, cast my vote, and made my voice heard! 💪🏾

Now it's your turn! 🇺🇸

#IVoted #EarlyVoting #BeTheChange
#ExerciseYourRightToVote #CastYourBallot

author: gailrenae333

item.authorHandle: gailrenae333
item.caption:
🙏🏼🙏🏼PRAY FOR ME🙏🏼🙏🏼

I’m in the early voting line. It’s looking like an hour wait. 
I have a dumocrat behind me and I’m trying to politely shut him up🤣
He’s loud. I said you ought not to talk any party in line.
Anchorage Ak
